newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkish PM coalition shows cracks under army push.
newsitem.headline: Turkish PM coalition shows cracks under army push.

text.p: Turkish Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan on Sunday called for an end to speculation that his Islamist-led coalition is in danger of splitting over army demands for a crackdown on religious activism.
"This country belongs to all of us. There is no need for artificial agendas and unnecessary tensions," Anatolian news agency quoted him as telling a meeting of his Islam-based Welfare Party.

The run-up to Monday's regularly scheduled meeting of the military-dominated National Security Council (NSC) touched off a war of words at the weekend between the coalition's Islamist and secularist wings.
Erbakan, the first Islamist leader of the officially secular republic, urged an end to such debate.
"Ways of developing the country should be discussed instead of short-sighted rows. We have to use our heads and do what has to be done in a democracy," he said.
At issue are 18 directives from the Council, charged under the constitution with safeguarding the secular system, aimed at choking off the growing influence of Islamists in public life.

Laid down on February 28, they include strict limits on Koranic education, enforcement of restrictions on headscarves and other forms of Moslem dress, as well as an assault on pro-Islamist media and business.
But the broader underlying questions -- the role of the military in Turkish democracy, relations between mosque and state and the rise of civil society -- are also in play.
Erbakan has reluctantly endorsed the Council's orders for a crackdown. However, Welfare aides have since hinted that enforcement would be less than enthusiastic.
The more outspoken ministers of the junior partner True Path Party, secularist conservatives at least in name, meanwhile pledged aggressive implementation of the army demands.
"Either this government will go, or democracy will," said commentator Bilal Cetin, summing up the the long-term outlook of a number of analysts.
"The consensus is that the chances of survival for both are decreasing steadily," Cetin wrote in the daily Yeni Yuzyil.

For the second time in a month the government cancelled its weekly cabinet meeting, apparently to avoid a public rift before the session of the National Security Council, which groups the top force commanders and senior government officials.
Talk of early elections, never far from the surface in Turkey, is once again in the air.
The agenda for Monday's meeting, which begins at 0630 GMT, has not been made public.

But enforcement of the February 28 orders, most notably cuts in the religious education that the Islam-based Welfare Party sees as vital to its future growth, is expected to be discussed under the catch-all of "national security."
Already there have been feverish preparations on all sides.

The military brass held a series of consultations late last week and press leaks indicate the army, by far the most respected institution in Turkey, is prepared to see off any protests from Prime Minister Erbakan.
At the same time True Path and Welfare officials, in uneasy coalition since June, 1996, have traded tough talk.

"The NSC decisions will be enforced to the letter. If there is anyone who is trying to stop that, let them come forward and try," said Yalim Erez, trade and industry minister from the True Path Party.
